newsitem.title: USA: White House busy with second term, Democratic flap.
newsitem.headline: White House busy with second term, Democratic flap.

text.p: As President Bill Clinton plays in Australia, the White House is looking at candidates for second-term jobs and trying to put out a fire fanned by a Democratic fund-raising scandal.

White House officials said Clinton's top priority on his return from a 12-day Asia tour will be naming his national security team including secretaries of state and defence after leaving town without filling those critical positions.

"We are in the final stages of consideration for some of the national security posts and the president plans to consider that as his first order of business when he returns, simultaneous with his national economic policy team," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

McCurry would not discuss names but other officials said the list for secretary of state still includes former Sen. George Mitchell of Maine and U.S. ambassador to the U.N. Madeleine Albright, among others.
On other jobs, they said members of a transition team have fanned out across the country consulting with community leaders about possible candidates.

In some cases, the team has begun preliminary checks on individuals who might be recommended to the president. This has led to speculative reports -- including one that Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell was favoured for a Cabinet position.

While that work continues, the White House has found itself on the defensive over the fallout from activities of John Huang, who raised $2.5 million in contributions for the Democratic Party, $600,000 of which has been returned because of questions as to whether it came from foreign sources.
The New York Times, in an editorial on Wednesday, urged Attorney General Janet Reno to name a special counsel to investigate the affair. She has already said she would not.

The Times also unleashed a blistering attack on a top Clinton confidant, Bruce Lindsey, as well as McCurry. It had reported on Tuesday that Lindsey successfully fended off two White House lawyers who wanted Clinton to admit that two Oval Office meetings with Indonesian billionaire James Riady, who once employed Huang, were not just social visits but included discussion of trade policy toward Indonesia and China.
Of the two lawyers, Mark Fabiani has departed as he had planned and Jane Sherburne is on her way out for reasons unrelated to the current controversy.

In its editorial, the newspaper said if Lindsey did lead the White House to misrepresent the facts he should resign as deputy White House counsel. It said McCurry "was left with his reliability in tatters" for describing the meetings as purely social.

McCurry, asked to comment, said some elements of the Times' account of the Lindsey story were exaggerated and some were untrue. He described Lindsey as particularly helpful in getting answers to press questions.
"I think he's been unfairly portrayed," McCurry said.
